lead: This unit teaches you to fix direction and position on the ground: meridians and bearings, the compass and its errors, the plane table, and the traverse computation that turns field measurements into coordinates. After it you can convert any bearing, correct a compass traverse for local attraction, run and adjust a closed traverse, and compute its area from coordinates.
about: Unit 2 is about direction: how a survey line is measured against north, how a compass reads it, how a plane table draws it, and how a set of such lines closes and is adjusted. Chapter 2.1 fixes the vocabulary of meridians, bearings and azimuths. Chapter 2.2 measures bearings with a compass and removes local attraction. Chapter 2.3 plots directions graphically on a plane table. Chapter 2.4 turns every bearing into a latitude and a departure, and Chapter 2.5 turns the leftover gap into corrections for the whole traverse. Chapter 2.6 closes with area from coordinates. The chapters build in that order: none of them can be done well without the one before it.

chapters.idea: Every direction in surveying is an angle measured from a chosen north, and the same line can be written in several equivalent ways that must agree.
chapters.depth: Define meridian and its four kinds: true (geographic), magnetic, grid and arbitrary. Define bearing and azimuth; note that some syllabi call the whole circle bearing measured clockwise from true north the azimuth. Cover whole circle bearing (WCB, 0° to 360°) and reduced or quadrantal bearing (RB, 0° to 90° with N or S first and E or W last), with the four conversion rules and the reverse conversions. Cover fore bearing and back bearing, FB − BB = 180°, interior angles between two lines at a station, magnetic declination, its yearly change, isogonic and agonic lines, and true bearing = magnetic bearing ± declination. Keep the arithmetic in degrees and minutes.

figure.aria: A decision tree that splits whole circle bearings into four quadrants and gives the reduced bearing rule for each one.

chapters.example: Convert WCB 145° and WCB 250° into reduced bearings and give the back bearing of each. Then a line has magnetic bearing 40°00′ and the declination at that place is 5°30′ east; find its true bearing and the true bearing of the opposite direction. Answers: 145° gives S 35° E with back bearing 325°; 250° gives S 70° W with back bearing 70°. True bearing = 40°00′ + 5°30′ = 45°30′; the opposite direction is 225°30′ true.
chapters.trap: Mixing the letters: the reference end (N or S) comes first and the direction (E or W) comes last, and the numbers must add up inside the quadrant. The second trap is adding the declination with the wrong sign, or forgetting that 1° = 60′ when adding minutes.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: angles, scales, maps and topographic sheets.
chapters.leave: The latitude and departure arithmetic belongs to 2.4. Measuring declination and handling the compass belongs to 2.2. Drawing meridians on a projected map belongs to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A compass gives the bearing of a line from magnetic north, but iron and electric current nearby pull the needle, so observed bearings must be tested and corrected before they are used.
chapters.depth: Parts of the surveyor's compass and the prismatic compass, least count (30′ for the prismatic compass), temporary adjustments, and how a bearing is read. Compass traverse: closed and open, bearings of all lines, then interior angles at each station. The two checks: FB − BB = 180° for every line, and sum of interior angles = (2n − 4) × 90° for a closed polygon of n sides. Local attraction: what causes it, how a station free from it is detected, and the two correction routes (interior angle method and the direct method from an unaffected line). Finish with sources of error and precautions. Keep theodolite work out of this chapter.
chapters.aria: A flow chart of the interior angle method: observed bearings give interior angles, the angle sum is checked, the error is shared, and corrected bearings are computed and back-checked.
chapters.example: Observed bearings of a closed traverse ABCD are AB 46°00′, BA 226°00′, BC 130°00′, CB 310°00′, CD 220°30′, DC 40°00′, DA 309°30′, AD 130°00′. Find the stations free from local attraction, the correction at each affected station, and all corrected bearings. Answer: AB and BA differ by 180° and BC and CB differ by 180°, so stations A and B are free. Readings at D are 30′ too small, so add 30′ at D: CD 220°30′, DC 40°30′, DA 310°00′, AD 130°00′. Angle check: 96° + 89°30′ + 90°30′ + 84° = 360°.
chapters.trap: Assuming the station at the start of the traverse is free. Only a line whose fore and back bearings differ by exactly 180° proves two stations free. The second trap is applying the station correction to bearings taken at other stations.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for bearings, back bearings and interior angles; Unit 1 for angular units and the ideas of error and precision.
chapters.leave: Angle measurement with a theodolite and theodolite traversing go to Unit 4. Plotting the corrected traverse goes to 2.5, and magnetic declination measurement is a field exercise of 2.1.

chapters.idea: Plane table surveying draws the map in the field, plotting each direction as a ray on the sheet, so no field book and no separate angle record are needed.
chapters.depth: Equipment: tripod, drawing board, alidade (plain and telescopic), spirit level, trough compass, plumbing fork and plumb bob, chain or tape. Setting up in the correct order: fixing, levelling, centring and orientation (magnetic, by trough compass, or by backsight on a plotted line). The four methods: radiation, intersection (triangulation), traversing and resection, with the field conditions that suit each. Two-point and three-point problems; for the three-point problem give the trial and error idea, Bessel's solution and Lehmann's rules at the level that syllabi usually ask, and say that some syllabi want the full construction. Advantages, disadvantages, common errors and precautions.
chapters.aria: Three known ground points A, B and C with three rays drawn from the table station P; the rays meet the plotted triangle and fix P on the sheet.
chapters.example: The line pq was already plotted on the sheet with a magnetic bearing of 210°. The table is set up at p and the trough compass needle along pq reads 195°. (a) By how much and in which direction must the table be turned? (b) What will the needle read along pq after correct orientation? Answer: pq is 15° short of its true magnetic bearing, so turn the table 15° clockwise until the needle along pq reads 210°. The correction is 15°.
chapters.trap: Confusing orientation with centring. Levelling and centring are done once at a station; orientation must be repeated at every new station, and the table is turned, never the plotted line.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for meridian and bearing; Chapter 2.2 for the trough compass; Unit 1 for scale and plotting.
chapters.leave: The plotting of the finished traverse sheet is in 2.5. Resection by least squares and the algebra of control networks belong to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Every traverse line splits into a north–south part called latitude and an east–west part called departure, and these parts add up like vectors.
chapters.depth: Define traverse, and the closed, open and link types with their field uses (road, canal, boundary). Latitude of a line of length l at whole circle bearing θ is l cos θ; departure is l sin θ, with θ always measured clockwise from north. Give the sign table by quadrant. Show how the same numbers come from reduced bearings with separate signs. Build a traverse table with columns for line, length, bearing, latitude and departure. Consecutive (dependent) coordinates from a starting station, and independent coordinates from a grid. The two checks for a closed traverse: Σ latitude = 0 and Σ departure = 0. Area is not done here.

figure.title: Traverse ABCD: length in m, bearing from north, latitude and departure in m

chapters.aria: A traverse table with one row per line showing length, bearing, latitude and departure, and a last row whose totals do not quite reach zero.
chapters.example: A closed traverse ABCD has AB 200 m at 45°, BC 180 m at 135°, CD 160 m at 210° and DA 226 m at 303°20′. Compute the latitude and departure of every line and the two sums. Answers: AB +141.42, +141.42; BC −127.28, +127.28; CD −138.56, −80.00; DA +124.08, −188.89. Σ latitude = −0.34 m and Σ departure = −0.19 m, which is not zero, so the traverse has a misclosure.
chapters.trap: Putting the reduced bearing into l cos θ and l sin θ. The formula needs the whole circle bearing, otherwise the signs of the latitude and departure come out wrong.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for whole circle bearings; Unit 1 for trigonometric ratios and coordinate axes.
chapters.leave: The misclosure itself and its correction are 2.5. Plotting the coordinates is in 2.5, and grid systems and datums are in Unit 1 and Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A closed traverse never closes exactly, so the gap is measured as the closing error and then spread over the lines by a fixed rule.
chapters.depth: Closing error e = √(ΣL² + ΣD²) and its bearing from tan θ = ΣD / ΣL, taking the signs to pick the quadrant. Relative precision = perimeter ÷ e, and permissible limits for compass and theodolite work. Angular misclosure against (2n − 4) × 90°, and the difference between angular and linear misclosure. Bowditch (compass) rule: correction to latitude of a line = −ΣL × (line length ÷ perimeter), and the same with ΣD for departure; state why it suits compass work. Transit rule as the alternative, and the equal or arbitrary method in one line. Then recompute the coordinates and prove both sums become zero. Some syllabi add omitted measurements, where one length or one bearing is missing; keep that to a short section and say so. Mention that the least squares adjustment exists and that only a few universities teach it at this level.
chapters.aria: The traverse runs A, B, C, D and ends at A prime instead of A; the short vector between them is the closing error of 0.39 m.
chapters.example: For the traverse AB 200 m at 45°, BC 180 m at 135°, CD 160 m at 210°, DA 226 m at 303°20′, with ΣL = −0.34 m and ΣD = −0.19 m, find the closing error, its bearing and the relative precision, then adjust by the Bowditch rule and give the final coordinates of A, B, C and D, taking A as (1000.00 E, 1000.00 N). Answer: e = √(0.34² + 0.19²) = 0.39 m; tan θ = 0.19/0.34 = 0.559 with both sums negative, so the bearing is 180° + 29° = 209°, roughly south-west. Perimeter = 766 m, precision ≈ 1 in 1960. Corrections to latitude: AB +0.09, BC +0.08, CD +0.07, DA +0.10 m. Corrections to departure: AB +0.05, BC +0.04, CD +0.04, DA +0.06 m. Adjusted coordinates: A (1000.00, 1000.00), B (1141.47, 1141.51), C (1268.79, 1014.31), D (1188.83, 875.82), closing back on A exactly.
chapters.trap: Dividing the misclosure by the number of lines instead of by the perimeter in the Bowditch rule, and applying a correction in the same direction as the error instead of opposite to it. The correction to latitude is −ΣL × (l ÷ P): ΣL is already negative, so the correction comes out positive.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for latitudes, departures and coordinates; Chapter 2.2 for angular misclosure.
chapters.leave: Weights, the normal equation method and least squares belong to Unit 4. Plotting the adjusted coordinates is in 2.5, and the same adjustments inside software appear in Unit 5 and Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Once every corner of a closed boundary has coordinates, the area inside comes out of one sum of cross products, with no need to draw the figure.
chapters.depth: Area by coordinates in both forms: twice the area equals the sum of E × (N_next − N_prev) taken around the boundary, and twice the area equals the sum of (E_i × N_next − E_next × N_i). Insist on taking the corners in order, clockwise or anticlockwise, and on the sign of the answer being fixed by the direction of travel. Work the arithmetic in a table so the examiner can see the method. Give the units: square metre, hectare (1 ha = 10 000 m²) and acre (1 acre = 4046.86 m²). Give double meridian distance as the older alternative name and method in brief. Note that the coordinates may come from a traverse, a total station, or a GNSS receiver, and that CAD and GIS compute this instantly (Unit 5 and Unit 7).

figure.title: Corners in order, eastings and northings in m; last column = E × (N_next − N_prev)

chapters.aria: A coordinate table for the four corners of a plot with the cross-product term for each corner and a total of 1100, which is twice the area.
chapters.example: Find the area of the plot ABCD with corners A(10, 10), B(30, 10), C(40, 30) and D(20, 40), eastings and northings in metres, taken in order around the boundary. Check the answer with the other form of the formula. Answer: 10 × (10 − 40) = −300; 30 × (30 − 10) = 600; 40 × (40 − 10) = 1200; 20 × (10 − 30) = −400. Sum = 1100, so area = 550 m² = 0.055 ha. Cross-product check: (10 × 10 − 30 × 10) + (30 × 30 − 40 × 10) + (40 × 40 − 20 × 30) + (20 × 10 − 10 × 40) = −200 + 500 + 1000 − 200 = 1100, the same.
chapters.trap: Taking the corners out of order or skipping one, which gives a bow-tie shape and a wrong area. The second trap is that the raw sum is twice the area, so students report double the correct value.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for coordinates and Chapter 2.5 for adjusted coordinates; Unit 1 for area units.
chapters.leave: Areas and volumes from contours and reservoir capacity are in Unit 3. Digital area computation, buffers and overlays are in Unit 7.
